name: Qwo (collagenase)

lead: Qwo is an enzyme injection given by clinicians to treat cellulite dimples on the buttocks of adult women with moderate to severe cellulite, for smoother-looking skin.

It uses a bacterial collagenase that cuts collagen in the fibrous bands under the skin that tether it and form dimples; the enzyme mostly stays at the injection site. A Phase 3 long-term study of 483 patients is registered, and later studies focus on reducing bruising.

paras: It is a prescription treatment injected in a clinic, in sessions spaced apart. Some physicians have also used it off-label on thighs.
Bruising is a prominent effect. The parent collagenase product lists pain, swelling, itching and rare allergic reactions. It is prescription-only and given in clinics.

angle.text: It is an injectable approved for cellulite dimples on women's buttocks: the enzyme breaks the fibrous bands pulling the skin down, so dimples release and the area looks smoother. Clinical trials studied dimple improvement, with bruising the main studied concern.

lead: Qwo (collagenase clostridium histolyticum-aaes, or CCH-aaes) is an injectable enzyme treatment for cellulite, made by Endo Aesthetics and approved as a subcutaneous injection for moderate to severe cellulite on the buttocks of adult women.[1][2] It is aimed at the visible dimpling of the skin over the buttocks and thighs: the enzymes are intended to cut the fibrous septae under the skin whose tension is thought to pull the surface into dimples, so that the skin looks smoother.[2]

Qwo belongs to the bacterial collagenase family that Endo also markets as Xiaflex for Dupuytren contracture and Peyronie disease; Wikipedia lists Qwo among the trade names of the parent substance.[3] Because that substance has been used medically since 2010, the safety profile of collagenase injections is better documented than that of many aesthetic procedures, though the cellulite formulation has its own bruising profile.[3][4]

Clinicians have described using it beyond the labeled site, on the thighs, and diluted beyond the proprietary diluent supplied with the product.[1][2] A Phase 3 long-term study of 483 participants and several Phase 2 and Phase 4 studies on reducing bruising are registered.[5][4][6][7] Cellulite is common and has no single established treatment; a 2025 systematic review of 24 randomised trials covering 2,084 patients compared mechanical, topical, shock wave, laser, radiofrequency, injectable and ultrasound approaches.[8]
infobox: Moderate to severe cellulite of the buttocks in adult women

paras: Cellulite, also called edematous fibrosclerotic panniculopathy in the clinical literature, is the uneven, dimpled look of skin, most often on the buttocks and thighs of women.[5][8] A widely discussed model is that fibrous septae anchor the skin to deeper tissue while fat bulges between them, so releasing the bands is a logical target.[2] Procedures aimed at that idea range from subcision with needles to injected enzymes. Reviewers note that a variety of modalities exist and that none is definitively established.[8]

Collagenase clostridium histolyticum is a mixture of two collagenases, derived from the bacterium Clostridium histolyticum, that cut collagen at different sites; the enzymes largely stay at the injection site.[3] In cellulite the target is the collagen-rich septae under the skin.[2]

Qwo is given by a clinician as a series of small subcutaneous injections across the treatment area, as described in the product's approved use for buttocks.[1][2] Early clinical-practice reports from aesthetic physicians describe treating both buttocks and thighs, and some practices dilute the supplied powder further than the proprietary diluent allows; a 2021 paper evaluated alternative diluents for that purpose.[1][2] A small Phase 4 study registered five participants to test multiple doses and concentrations for mild to moderate cellulite.[9]
Because bruising is prominent after treatment, practitioners and the manufacturer have registered studies on ways to limit it, including an oral tranexamic acid study.[4][6][7]

A Phase 3 long-term study (NCT03526549) of CCH-aaes in cellulite enrolled 483 participants and is registered as completed.[5] Phase 4 and Phase 2 studies have examined ways to reduce bruising after buttock injections, including oral tranexamic acid (17 participants) and other mitigation treatments (48 and 91 participants).[4][6][7] A small Phase 4 study (5 participants) tested multiple doses and concentrations.[9] The registry entries do not publish efficacy results in their summaries. A 2022 article summarised early clinical-practice experience treating buttocks and thighs,[2] and a 2021 paper evaluated alternative diluents.[1]

In the 2025 systematic review of cellulite treatments, shock wave therapy showed a consistent score reduction across four studies, and radiofrequency also showed a statistically significant reduction; the review evaluated subcutaneous injectables as one of several categories.[8] Follow-up in the included trials averaged a little over three weeks.[8]

The existence of multiple studies aimed at bruising mitigation indicates bruising is a prominent effect of buttock injections.[4][6][7] For the parent collagenase product, Wikipedia lists swollen lymph nodes, itching, pain, swelling and bruising or bleeding as common effects, with allergic reactions in under 1 percent of patients.[3] For Peyronie disease treatment with Xiaflex, penile fracture and other serious penile injury are recognised risks, which do not apply to the buttock indication.[3]

Xiaflex was approved by the US FDA in February 2010 as the first non-surgical treatment for Dupuytren contracture, and in December 2013 for Peyronie disease following an application by Auxilium.[3] Auxilium reported that trials of Xiaflex for cellulite were underway.[3] Endo Pharmaceuticals markets Xiaflex in the US, and Sobi marketed it in Europe as Xiapex until withdrawing distribution for commercial reasons in March 2020.[3]

Other cellulite approaches studied in randomised trials include mechanical stimulation, topical therapy, laser and light devices, radiofrequency and acoustic wave therapy.[8] Collagenase is also researched for fibrotic conditions such as Dupuytren contracture, where a 2024 randomised trial compared collagenase injection with limited fasciectomy.[10]

timeline.event: FDA approves Xiaflex for Dupuytren contracture.[3]
FDA approves Xiaflex for Peyronie disease.[3]
Phase 3 long-term cellulite study NCT03526549 starts.[5]
Sobi withdraws Xiapex distribution in Europe; Phase 4 bruising study begins.[3][6]
Early clinical-practice experience on buttocks and thighs reported.[2]
